A close reading for the week

“This can be no trick”

Much Ado About Nothing · Act 2, Scene 3

It is a trick. Benedick has just overheard his friends staging a conversation for his benefit, and steps out of the arbour to reason himself, clause by clause, from confirmed bachelor to man in love. He deceives himself thoroughly, and it makes him happy.

BenedickAdvancing from the arbour.This can be no trick: the conference was sadly borne.1 They have the truth of this from Hero. They seem to pity the lady: it seems her affections have their full bent. Love me? why, it must be requited.2 I hear how I am censured: they say I will bear myself proudly, if I perceive the love come from her; they say too that she will rather die than give any sign of affection.

  1. 1

    No trick

    “This can be no trick,” says Benedick, and the audience has just watched the trick performed. His evidence is that the conversation was “sadly borne”, conducted gravely; his friends, in other words, acted well. The comedy of the whole speech is dramatic irony at full stretch: every inference he draws is reasonable, the premise is false, and the result is the truth anyway, because he does love her.

  2. 2

    The pivot

    “Love me? why, it must be requited.” The question is astonishment; the answer arrives in the same breath, before any deliberation. Benedick decides in four words, and spends the rest of the speech constructing reasons for a decision already made. Shakespeare knew that this is how people persuade themselves: the conclusion first, the argument after.
